         TEXAS OIL & GAS ASSOCIATION COMMENTS TO PROPOSAL FOR
                     PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC §25.194


The Texas Oil & Gas Association (TXOGA) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments to
the discussion draft §25.194 as part of Project 58481 by the Public Utility Commission of Texas
(Commission). This draft would set forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility, including a
municipally owned utility and electric cooperative, to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT
transmission network. The Commission’s proposal for publication invites comments by December
19, 2025. As such these comments are timely filed.


TXOGA is a statewide trade association representing every facet of the Texas oil and gas industry
including small independents and major producers. Collectively, the membership of TXOGA
produces approximately 90 percent of Texas’ crude oil and natural gas and operates the vast
majority of the state’s refineries and pipelines. In fiscal year 2024, the Texas oil and natural gas
industry supported over 490,000 direct jobs and paid $27.3 billion in state and local taxes and state
royalties, funding our state’s schools, roads and first responders.


As one of the most electricity-intensive industries in Texas, the oil and natural gas sector has a
vested interest in interconnection standards for large load customers.
 COMMENTS BY SECTION:


§ 25.194(a). Purpose and Scope.


Proposed § 25.194(a) states that the purpose and scope of the rule are to establish “standards and
criteria for an electric utility … to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT transmission
network.” This framing is important, because it confirms that § 25.194 is an interconnection rule,
not a regime governing the ongoing operation or dispatchability of retail load after interconnection
has been completed.


TXOGA recognizes that the rapid influx of large loads presents legitimate reliability
considerations for the ERCOT system, and that appropriate standards or mechanisms may be
necessary to ensure that such loads do not create undue reliability risks. However, the
Commission’s consideration of those issues must occur within a regulatory framework that is
consistent with PURA, provides due process, and clearly allocates authority among the
Commission, utilities, and ERCOT. As discussed in the comments on § 25.194(l) below, several
provisions of the draft rule—most notably the authorization for ERCOT to impose “operational
standards” as a condition of continued operation—extend beyond the interconnection-focused
scope articulated in subsection (a).


Conditioning continued retail electric service on compliance with ERCOT-developed operational
requirements exceeds the stated purpose of § 25.194 and underscores that subsection (l) cannot be
reconciled with the rule’s own scope limitation or with PURA § 37.0561. If the Commission
determines that additional ongoing performance or controllability requirements for large loads are
warranted, those requirements should be evaluated through a separate, transparent rulemaking that
addresses registration status, enforcement authority, and procedural protections, rather than
through an interconnection rule focused on utility obligations.


§ 25.194(j). Reallocation of capacity.


Section 25.194(j) establishes a mandatory reallocation mechanism when a large load customer
fails to meet phased energization milestones within 18 months. This is a significant enforcement
tool that already exposes large load customers to loss of capacity and financial consequences for
delay or nonperformance.
 For institutional oil and gas customers with long-cycle, capital-intensive facilities, reallocation risk
is particularly acute, as development timelines are often driven by commodity markets, permitting,
and upstream or midstream coordination rather than by speculative development strategies. When
combined with the layered financial security and CIAC requirements elsewhere in § 25.194,
subsection (j) already creates substantial downside exposure.


The addition of ERCOT operational standards under § 25.194(l) compounds this risk by
introducing a separate, open-ended compliance regime that could affect continued operation even
after energization. Read together, subsections (j) and (l) transform § 25.194 from an
interconnection framework into an ongoing regulatory regime governing retail load, without the
statutory clarity, procedural safeguards, or Commission oversight that would ordinarily
accompany such a regime, and in a manner that is inconsistent with PURA § 37.0561(b)’s directive
to minimize stranded infrastructure costs and support business development.


§25.194(l). ERCOT operational standards.
    (1) ERCOT may establish operational standards for large load customers to ensure system
        reliability.
    (2) A large load customer must comply with operational standards, developed through
        ERCOT protocols, as a condition for interconnection and continued operation of the
        customer’s load.


TXOGA believes §25.194(l), as proposed, is unnecessary, legally ambiguous, and conflicts with
existing provisions of the Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA). The proposed language must be
interpreted narrowly and strictly in context of the definition of “large load customer” in paragraph
(b)(7) of the discussion draft, which mirrors PURA §37.0561. Accordingly, any operational
standards adopted pursuant to §25.194(l) may apply only prospectively to new or expanded
interconnection requests and may not be applied retroactively to existing customers absent a
request for expanded service.


The provision also appears to expand ERCOT’s authority beyond what is expressly granted under
PURA §39.151. TXOGA believes that this expansion of authority would represent a significant
shift in how large load customers are treated within the ERCOT market. PURA §39.151 authorizes
ERCOT to ensure reliability through market rules and protocols applicable to market participants
but does not grant ERCOT independent authority to impose operational performance obligations
 directly on end-use customers as a condition of continued service. This represents a material
departure from longstanding regulatory treatment of firm load in ERCOT. Industrial facilities—
including oil and natural gas operations—have historically relied on predictable firm-load
treatment to support long-lived, capital-intensive investments. Introducing open-ended operational
standards risks undermining this certainty and could have unintended economic and safety
consequences.


Stakeholders have expressed concern that the proposed language grants ERCOT broad and largely
unbounded discretion to define what is required “to ensure system reliability” without clear
statutory guardrails or Commission oversight. TXOGA further emphasizes that many industrial
facilities cannot safely modulate operations in response to real-time grid conditions. Imposing
operational requirements designed for generation or controllable load resources could jeopardize
personnel safety, equipment integrity, and public safety.


Market participants are compensated for reliability services and are subject to operational
standards as a condition of receiving market revenues. Large load customers are not similarly
compensated and do not participate in ERCOT markets. Large load customers already fund grid
reliability through transmission cost recovery, ancillary service charges, congestion rents, and
uplift. Imposing operational standards on large load customers--without compensation or clear
statutory authority--would blur the distinction between customers and market participants and
create a fundamentally inequitable regulatory outcome TXOGA believes that establishing similar
operational requirements for large load customers would be inappropriate, given the structural
distinctions between these customers and other market participants.


For these reasons, TXOGA urges the Commission to delete §25.194(l). While we strongly oppose
the inclusion of operational standards on industrial customers, if any similar provisions were to be
proposed there must be clarity surrounding any operational standards to ensure they apply only
prospectively to new or expanded interconnections; do not alter firm-load treatment absent explicit
statutory authorization; and, are narrowly tailored, safety-conscious, and subject to Commission
oversight.
 TXOGA appreciates the opportunity to comment and looks forward to continued engagement with
the Commission and stakeholders to implement SB6 in a manner that preserves reliability while
supporting Texas’ industrial competitiveness and economic growth.



Respectfully submitted,




Matt Patterson
Director of Government and Regulatory Affairs
Texas Oil & Gas Association

              TEXAS OIL & GAS ASSOCIATION EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


The Texas Oil & Gas Association (TXOGA) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments
on the discussion draft proposal for new 16 TAC §25.194. As described in greater detail in our
comments we recommend:

•   TXOGA recognizes that the rapid influx of large loads presents legitimate reliability
    considerations for the ERCOT system, but consideration of those issues must occur within a
    regulatory framework that is consistent with PURA, provides due process, and clearly allocates
    authority among the Commission, utilities, and ERCOT. Section 25.194(l) extends beyond the
    interconnection-focused scope articulated in §25.194(a).
•   Section 25.194(j) is a significant enforcement tool that already exposes large load customers
    to loss of capacity and financial consequences for delay or nonperformance.

•   TXOGA believes the proposed §25.194(l) is unnecessary and conflicts with existing provisions
    of PURA. This provision would expand ERCOT’s authority beyond what is currently
    authorized under PURA §39.151.

•   Any ERCOT operational standards established under this provision must align with the
    definition of large load customer in PURA §37.0561 and should not apply retroactively to
    existing large load customers.
•   The proposed change could undermine longstanding assumptions about “firm load” treatment
    for large customers above certain thresholds.

•   There are significant safety concerns for industrial facilities attempting to meet operational
    standards that are not applicable to existing entities.

•   Market participants are compensated for participation and are appropriately subject to
    operational and reliability standards, while large load customers are fundamentally different:
    they pay for grid reliability through transmission, ancillary services, and also pay congestion
    costs. Imposing similar operational requirements on large load customers would ignore these
    structural and economic distinctions.
